name: Battle of Red Cliffs
info: In the winter of 208–209 CE the allied forces of Sun Quan, Liu Bei and Liu Qi defeated the larger army of the northern warlord Cao Cao on the Yangtze, halting his advance south and leaving China divided.

facts.date: Winter of 208–209 CE; historians differ on the timeline of events
facts.place: On the Yangtze River in Jing Province, China; the exact site is disputed, with candidates southwest of present-day Wuhan and near Chibi City in Hubei
facts.sides: The allies Sun Quan (commander Zhou Yu), Liu Bei and Liu Qi, about 50,000 marines in all, against Cao Cao, who claimed 800,000 men while Zhou Yu estimated about 230,000
facts.outcome: The allies drove Cao Cao's fleet and army back; Cao Cao escaped north and never again commanded so large a fleet, while Liu Bei and Sun Quan kept the lands south of the Yangtze.

t: Cao Cao's southern campaign, begun in the autumn of 208, brought him Jiangling and a large fleet before it was halted on the Yangtze.
The allies fought on the river, and a feigned surrender by Huang Gai set Cao Cao's chained ships ablaze.
The battle fixed the Yangtze as a frontier, the basis of the later states of Shu Han and Eastern Wu, though its exact site is still disputed.
dyk: Cao Cao wrote to Sun Quan claiming an army of 800,000, while Zhou Yu put his strength nearer 230,000, including between 70 and 80 thousand men impressed from Ying.
ev: Cao Cao defeats his main rival Yuan Shao at Guandu and gains control of the North China Plain
Cao Cao defeats the Wuhuan at White Wolf Mountain, securing his northern flank
Cao Cao's southern campaign begins in the autumn; Liu Cong surrenders Jiangling and a sizeable fleet to him
Liu Bei is defeated at Changban and retreats east; Zhuge Liang negotiates an alliance with Sun Quan
The allied fleet meets Cao Cao's vanguard at Red Cliffs, and Huang Gai's fire ships set Cao Cao's fleet ablaze
Cao Cao retreats along Huarong Road; Jiangling falls to Zhou Yu by the end of the year
Zhou Yu dies, weakening Sun Quan's position in Jing Province
The Three Kingdoms period begins, with Shu Han and Eastern Wu resting on the frontiers fixed at Red Cliffs

sections.background:
By the early 3rd century CE the Han dynasty, nearly four centuries old, was crumbling. Emperor Xian, who came to the throne in 189 at the age of eight, was a figurehead with no control over the regional warlords. Cao Cao, one of the most powerful of them, hosted the emperor at his capital at Ye, which gave him a measure of control over the emperor and an air of legitimacy. In 200 he defeated his main rival Yuan Shao at Guandu, which gave him the North China Plain, and in the winter of 207 he secured his northern flank by defeating the Wuhuan at White Wolf Mountain. After he returned to Ye in 208 he was appointed Chancellor on his own recommendation, which effectively gave him control of the imperial government.

His southern campaign began in the autumn of 208. The stretch of the Yangtze through Jing Province was the first target, because the naval base at Jiangling and naval control of that stretch of the river were necessary to secure access to the south. Jing was in a poor state: its armies were exhausted by conflict with Sun Quan, and Liu Biao's sons Liu Qi and Liu Cong were rivals to succeed their father. Liu Cong prevailed, Liu Biao died a few weeks later, and Liu Cong surrendered to the advancing Cao Cao, giving him a sizeable fleet and Jiangling as a forward base.
sections.forces:
Cao Cao's advance forced Liu Bei into a disorganised retreat south, accompanied by refugees and pursued by Cao Cao's elite cavalry. Liu Bei was surrounded and defeated at Changban but escaped east to Xiakou, where he met Sun Quan's emissary Lu Su. Zhuge Liang, Liu Bei's main adviser, went to Chaisang to negotiate an alliance with Sun Quan. He said that Liu Bei and Liu Qi each had 10,000 men, figures that may have been exaggerated. Cao Cao sent Sun Quan a letter claiming an army of 800,000 and hinting that he wanted surrender. Zhang Zhao, Sun Quan's chief clerk, favoured surrender; Lu Su and Zhou Yu, Sun Quan's chief commander, supported Zhuge Liang.

Sun Quan chose the alliance, reportedly cutting a corner off his desk and saying that anyone who still argued for surrender would be treated the same. Zhou Yu, Cheng Pu and Lu Su were given 30,000 men, and with Liu Bei's 20,000 soldiers the alliance had approximately 50,000 marines, trained and prepared for battle. Zhou Yu put Cao Cao's strength nearer 230,000, including between 70 and 80 thousand men impressed from Ying whose morale and loyalty were uncertain. Cao Cao's force also held non-combatants, among them supply and communications workers and the wives and children of some soldiers. His men were mostly cavalry and infantry with little naval experience, and he had only a few days of drills before the battle.
sections.course:
The battle opened with an attempt by Cao Cao's forces to establish a bridgehead across the Yangtze, which failed, and both sides drew back to their positions on either bank. The combined Sun and Liu force then sailed upstream from either Xiakou or Fankou to Red Cliffs and met Cao Cao's vanguard. Cao Cao's men, troubled by disease and low morale after forced marches, could not gain an advantage in the skirmish, and he withdrew to Wulin on the north bank while the allies pulled back south.

Cao Cao had chained his ships stem to stern, possibly to reduce seasickness among his mostly northern crews. Seeing this, the divisional commander Huang Gai sent Cao Cao a letter feigning surrender and prepared a squadron of ships filled with bundles of kindling, dry reeds and fatty oil. As the squadron neared the middle of the river its sailors lit the ships and took to small boats, and the unmanned fire ships, carried by the southeastern wind, set Cao Cao's fleet ablaze. Many men and horses burned to death or drowned. Zhou Yu and the allies then led a lightly armed force against the northern army, which fell into confusion, and Cao Cao ordered a general retreat, destroying a number of his remaining ships.
sections.aftermath:
Cao Cao's army retreated along Huarong Road, much of it through marshland north of Dongting Lake. Heavy rain had made the road so bad that many sick soldiers carried bundles of grass on their backs to fill it for the horsemen, and many drowned in the mud or were trampled. The allies, led by Zhou Yu and Liu Bei, pursued by land and water as far as Nan Commandery, and the chase, famine and disease ravaged what remained of Cao Cao's force. He went back north to Yecheng, leaving Cao Ren and Xu Huang at Jiangling, Yue Jin at Xiangyang and Man Chong at Dangyang. The allied pursuit lost momentum when the crossing dissolved into chaos as armies fought over the few ferries, and only a rearguard action by Cao Ren prevented a worse disaster. No casualty figures are given for either side.

By the end of 209 Jiangling fell to Zhou Yu, and the land Cao Cao held contracted by about 160 kilometres (99 mi) to the area around Xiangyang. Liu Qi was made Inspector of Jing Province but died a few months later, and his lands were mostly absorbed by Sun Quan. Liu Bei then claimed the title and took four commanderies south of the Yangtze: Wuling, Changsha, Lingling and Guiyang. Sun Quan's troops had suffered far greater casualties than Liu Bei's in the fighting against Cao Ren, and Zhou Yu's death in 210 weakened Sun Quan in Jing Province.
sections.sources:
Historians have reached different conclusions in reconstructing the timeline of events, and accounts of Lu Su's meeting with Liu Bei are inconsistent: he may have persuaded Liu Bei to move further east to Fankou. Every figure for the armies comes from the people involved: Cao Cao's claim of 800,000, Zhuge Liang's 10,000 each for Liu Bei and Liu Qi, and Zhou Yu's estimate of 230,000. Zhuge Liang's figures may have been exaggerated, and none of them is a count. Cao Cao's own comment on the defeat blames sickness, not the enemy: he said that it was only because of the sickness that he burned his ships and retreated, and that it was out of all reason for Zhou Yu to take the credit.

The location of the battlefield has never been conclusively established, and scholars have contested it for at least 1,350 years. Historical records place it on the southern bank, west of Fankou and downstream of Baqiu. Four locations are still advocated. Chibi Hill at Huangzhou, named in Su Dongpo's poem, has been dismissed by virtually all scholars. Chibi City, formerly Puqi, is possibly the most widely accepted candidate, with a case first made in the early Tang dynasty and cliff inscriptions at least 1,000 years old. Scholars who follow the Shui Jing Zhu, such as Rafe de Crespigny and Zhu Dongrun, place it at Jiayu County, and others argue for Wuhan. Changes in the river's course and in place names complicate the question.
sections.legacy:
The allied victory ensured the survival of Liu Bei and Sun Quan and left them in control of the Yangtze, establishing defensible frontiers that later served as the basis for the states of Shu Han and Eastern Wu in the Three Kingdoms period (220 to 280 CE). Cao Cao's effort to reunify the territories of the Eastern Han was frustrated, and he never again commanded so large a fleet or had so good an opportunity to destroy his southern rivals. The battle and Liu Bei's capture of Jing Province confirmed the separation of southern China from the northern heartland of the Yellow River valley and foreshadowed a north to south axis of hostility that would continue for centuries.

The battle has long been a subject of art. The Song poet Su Dongpo, while exiled to Huangzhou, composed three widely anthologised pieces on the Red Cliff theme, two fu rhapsodies and one ci lyric, and a memorial museum to him opened in Huanggang in 2010. Many video games set in the Three Kingdoms period feature the battle, among them the Dynasty Warriors series and Total War: Three Kingdoms. John Woo's 2008 film Red Cliff, an adaptation of the folk history surrounding the battle, set a new box office record for a domestically produced film on its release in China.

summary: In the winter of 208–209 CE the allied forces of Sun Quan, Liu Bei and Liu Qi turned back Cao Cao's southern campaign on the Yangtze, using fire ships against his chained fleet. The victory fixed a frontier that later became the basis of Shu Han and Eastern Wu.
notes: The article gives no casualty figures; none are stated.
Troop strengths are attributed to the participants (Cao Cao 800,000, Zhou Yu 230,000, Zhuge Liang 10,000 each); the article's 50,000 allied marines is given as approximate without attribution.

The article does not name the ancient texts the battle is known from (such as the Records of the Three Kingdoms), so the sources section cannot name them. It names the Jingzhou ji and Shui Jing Zhu only in the location debate; I used the Shui Jing Zhu and left the Jingzhou ji out for space.
'Ying' is as the article writes it, not explained.
I left out Zhuge Liang's arrow and silk saying and most of the Analysis section's explanation of Cao Cao's errors beyond the points in forces and sources.
